value: Cedar Relay retries only eligible failures
A retryability check stops permanent failures early, while exponential delays space out further attempts. Neither change guarantees exactly-once delivery.
Fictional change · Source and deterministic probe results
Based on the supplied source and modeled probes. No timing or production measurements; no separate verification findings were supplied.
One send, then a bounded retry budget

Cedar Relay wraps an asynchronous send operation with a retry loop. Previously, every rejection could trigger another attempt after a requested 10-millisecond delay. A successful send returned immediately; the final failed attempt threw its error.

The retries argument counts extra attempts. With a budget of two, you can make at most three sends. A zero budget still allows the initial send.
Permanent failures still got another attempt

Send errors carry a boolean retryable property, but the old loop ignored it. In the supplied permanent-failure probe, the first send rejects with retryable: false. The old implementation waits and sends again; the new implementation returns that error after one call, without sleeping.

This removes an unnecessary attempt when the caller has already classified the failure as permanent. It does not establish whether a rejected send already changed the remote system.
Keep the bound, filter the error, double the delay

The updated loop preserves the attempt budget and awaits each send:

{{CODE:0}}

Starting at zero makes the inclusive bound allow one initial attempt plus the configured retries. Returning the awaited result stops the loop on success.

The catch block now decides whether another attempt is eligible before requesting a delay:

{{CODE:1}}

A permanent error or exhausted budget throws immediately. Otherwise, the requested delays grow as 10, 20, 40 milliseconds, and so on. The exhaustion probe records three sends and delays of 10 and 20 milliseconds, versus 10 and 10 before. These are requested delays: the probe resolves sleep immediately. A rejected sleep propagates and prevents another send.
Better retry decisions, not exactly-once delivery

The change filters failures and increases retry delays within the existing budget. The author's exactly-once claim exceeds that mechanism: a remote effect can commit before a send rejects, and the duplicate probe records two effects in both implementations. There is no deduplication or idempotency contract. Separate calls also share neither a counter nor a lock; the concurrent probe records an effect from each call.
